content: Red man syndrome is a condition that manifests with symptoms resembling an anaphylactoid reaction. These symptoms include difficulty breathing (dyspnea), low blood pressure (hypotension), hives (urticaria), pain and muscle spasms in the chest and back, wheezing, itching (pruritus), and flushing of the upper body, which gives the characteristic appearance that led to the name red man syndrome. When the causative agent is discontinued, the symptoms can resolve as quickly as 20 minutes in some cases, though in others, resolution may take several hours. The most common cause of red man syndrome is the administration of vancomycin, particularly when infused over less than one hour in patients who have not been pre-treated with diphenhydramine. Other antibiotics that can trigger red man syndrome due to hypersensitivity include ciprofloxacin, amphotericin B, rifampicin, and teicoplanin. The symptoms associated with red man syndrome include headache, chills, low blood pressure (hypotension), dizziness, chest pain, difficulty breathing (dyspnea), itching (pruritus), hives (urticaria), and a rash. The rash is typically erythematous and involves the face, neck, and upper torso. Additional symptoms include muscle spasms in the chest and back, wheezing, and flushing of the upper body, which contributes to the syndrome's characteristic appearance. Red man syndrome shares features with an anaphylactoid reaction, which is a non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.
